Meeting header: 
Date: 2026-01-14 16:00 UTC | Duration: ~45m | Attendees: Maya Chen (Redwood AE), Carlos Rivera (Redwood SE), Priya Desai (CTO, DataLoom), Liam O'Connor (Lead Engineer), Sara Kim (PM)

Summary (auto): quick Hosted API chat/text gen intro focused on streaming behaviour, tuning params for cost/latency, and practical retry/backoff patterns. Demo of Console routing and a few Optimize suggestions. Action items and follow-up POC scoping planned.

[00:00:12] Maya: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Maya from Redwood, AE on this account, and with me is Carlos, our solutions engineer. How's it going?
[00:00:20] Priya: Good, thanks. Excited to see the streaming stuff — we're trying to improve our chat response UX and reduce tail latency.
[00:00:28] Carlos: Awesome. Quick agenda: we'll show a hosted API quickstart for chat gen, live streaming demo, talk about params like temperature/top_p/max_tokens, then go into retries/backoff and idempotency. We'll wrap with the Console + Optimize suggestions.
[00:00:42] Liam: Sounds good. For context, our current stack: in-house service calling OpenAI, about 200 rps during peak, average message length 120 tokens, heavy burstiness in morning. We have a few compliance constraints — SOC2 and SSO with SAML.
[00:00:57] Maya: Perfect. We'll call out mapping for SSO and our Private options later but for the hosted demo we'll focus on behavior.

[00:02:10] Carlos: Ok I'm going to share my screen — quick code snippet in Node. This is the streaming endpoint call: we open the SSE/WebSocket stream, receive chunks, append to the UI. Important piece: we include an idempotency token on the request so retries don't double-charge or duplicate outputs.
[00:02:30] Sara: Can you show the exact header name?
[00:02:35] Carlos: Yeah, we recommend X-Redwood-Idempotency or you can provide client_request_id. If a client reconnects we use that to dedupe on the server side. Sometimes the automatic SDK does that for you.
[00:03:05] Priya: How does that interact with streaming retries — like if a 503 happens in the middle of a stream?
[00:03:13] Carlos: Good question. Two patterns: 1) checkpoint + resume: client keeps the partial token offset and asks backend to resume from KV cache if available; 2) optimistic reconnect: client replays the request with same idempotency token and server either resumes or returns the complete response from cache. In hosted mode we try resume first for low latency.
[00:03:40] Liam: KV cache? you mean K V cache?
[00:03:44] Carlos: Yeah, sometimes transcript misc: KV cache — key value cache for prefix tokens (we said K V cash earlier in the docs). It's basically the cached KV layers of the model so you avoid recomputing earlier context on reconnects.

[00:05:00] Maya: Let's demo streaming live. I'll kick a sample request with temperature 0.2 and max_tokens 100 to show crisp completions — this is the sort of config DataLoom might use for factual assistant answers.
[00:05:15] [screen share — console + terminal]
[00:05:20] Carlos: You can see the SSE events coming through, small chunks, flushes every ~120-200ms. That chunk size is controlled by our runtime but you can tune client-side chunk aggregation to avoid UI jitter.
[00:05:40] Liam: What's the difference between low-latency chunking and throughput optimization?
[00:05:45] Carlos: Lower chunk intervals -> better perceived latency but higher overhead per token. For throughput it's better to buffer a little and process larger chunks. Redwood Optimize actually recommends batching params based on your traffic pattern — we'll show an example.

[00:07:30] Sara: Walk me through the main generation params again — temperature, top_p, and stop sequences — and examples for defaults?
[00:07:36] Carlos: Sure. Temperature controls randomness; 0–0.3 for deterministic QA, 0.7+ for creative. Top_p is nucleus sampling; often you only need one of the two. Max_tokens limits the completion length. Also we have 'max_new_tokens' semantics in some SDKs; be careful. Stop sequences are explicit tokens to cut output, useful to avoid hallucinated continuations.
[00:08:10] Priya: Is there a cost/per-token change when you stream vs non-stream?
[00:08:14] Maya: No, cost per token is the same; streaming is just a delivery mechanism. However, your client patterns and retries can cause duplicate consumption if not using idempotency, so that's where cost leaks happen.

[00:09:50] Carlos: Now, about retries: typical failure modes are 429 (rate limit), 503 (transient infra), 500 (server error). Best practice: for 429 and 503 use exponential backoff with jitter, limit total retry window to preserve UX. For streaming specifically we recommend a short reconnect strategy with checkpoint resume.
[00:10:15] Liam: Example backoff numbers?
[00:10:18] Carlos: Start with base 200ms, multiply by 2, cap at 5s, add full jitter. Stop after 3 retries for interactive chat. For non-interactive batch jobs you can be more aggressive.
[00:10:33] Sara: Do you expose 95p latency metrics in the Console?
[00:10:37] Maya: Yes — per-route dashboards include p50/p95/p99, token breakdown, and cost per 1k tokens. We also show retry counts and failed vs succeeded requests.

[00:12:00] Priya: On security: we need SOC2 evidence and SAML SSO integration. How does hosted handle log retention and audit trails?
[00:12:12] Maya: We can provide SOC2 reports. For hosted we have configurable audit log retention for enterprise, and you can forward logs to your SIEM. SAML is supported for Console access; for API auth we use API keys and support rotating keys via the Console.
[00:12:35] Priya: Good. Also data residency — can you pin region?
[00:12:39] Maya: Yes, in hosted we have region pinning for EU/NA, and if you need full private control we have Private deployments. We'll include a short doc on differences.

[00:14:10] Carlos: Back to streaming: here's a demo of failing mid-stream. I simulate a transient 503 after 60 tokens. Client reconnects with same idempotency token; server returns resume token and we pick up at 61. See how perceived latency is small.
[00:14:32] [demo shows resumed stream playback]
[00:14:40] Liam: Nice. What about deterministic outputs for tests — like we need consistent responses for our regression test suite.
[00:14:46] Carlos: For deterministic outputs use temperature=0, set seed where supported, and pin to a model version. Also Redwood has model version pinning in the Console and rollout controls for canarying. For tests, you can also snapshot completions via our Evaluations tooling.

[00:16:50] Sara: Can you show how Console helps with route configuration and fallback to a cheaper model?
[00:16:55] Maya: Sure — switching to Console view. In Routes you can set routing policies: priority by latency or cost, region failover, and auto-fallback chains (e.g., primary gpt-like-large, fallback small-quantized). We show metrics and cost estimates per route.
[00:17:30] Carlos: Optimize suggests quantized variants if your workload is mostly embeddings or small completions — that can cut unit cost. It also suggests batching windows based on observed inter-arrival times.

[00:18:50] Priya: Could Optimize suggest explicit batching size and the expected latency impact?
[00:18:55] Carlos: Yes. Example: with 200 rps and 50% burstiness Optimize suggested 20–30ms batching window to improve throughput without exceeding p95 SLO. We'll attach the Optimize export.

[00:20:05] Liam: If we pin to a dedicated pool later, does the client change?
[00:20:10] Maya: No API changes. The same REST/SDK calls work; routing changes under the hood. For Dedicated you get reserved GPUs and SLA-backed latency.

[00:22:00] Sara: We also want to know about token accounting — do you expose raw tokenization so we can precompute token cost?
[00:22:05] Carlos: We provide a tokenizer library and per-token cost breakdown in the Console. Note: different models tokenize slightly differently so cost per message can vary by model.

[00:24:20] Priya: Any gotchas in retries that cause duplicate user-visible output?
[00:24:25] Carlos: Yes — if you retry without idempotency and the original request actually completed, you'll get a second response. For streaming, replays can create interleaved chunks if you don't handle resume correctly. Use idempotency and server-side dedupe.

[00:26:40] Maya: Quick question for DataLoom: what's your success criteria for a POC? Is it p95 under X ms and cost under Y?
[00:26:50] Priya: Ideally p95 < 400ms for short answers and under $0.0007 per token effective cost. But we can be flexible — main thing is predictable tail latencies and stable cost per 1M tokens.
[00:27:06] Maya: Good, we'll document that as the target and tune routes and batching accordingly.

[00:28:55] Carlos: I'm going to paste an SDK snippet for streaming reconnection best practice into chat — sample backoff, idempotency header example, and a quick web UI aggregation approach.
[00:29:10] [chat: https://redwood.example/decks/hosted-quickstart | SDK: https://redwood.example/sdk/streaming-snippets]

[00:31:00] Liam: Question on monitoring during POC — can we forward traces to our datadog?
[00:31:05] Maya: Yes, we have hooks for distributed tracing and you can forward logs and metrics to Datadog, Splunk, or your SIEM. We'll share the configuration.

[00:33:20] Sara: Any limitations on maximum concurrent streaming connections per API key?
[00:33:25] Carlos: In hosted default limits apply, you can request quota increases. For Dedicated we provision based on reserved capacity. You can also use token-level quotas per route.

[00:35:05] Priya: On the legal side, we'll need the data processing addendum.
[00:35:10] Maya: We'll include DPA and SOC2 in the follow-up pack.

[00:36:40] Carlos: Quick note: for heavy throughput use-cases, prefer batching at the edge and using our bulk endpoints where appropriate — that reduces per-token latency variance and cost.

[00:38:00] Maya: Ok let's recap next steps and owners.
[00:38:06] Maya: Action items: I'll send sandbox key + quickstart; Carlos will send backoff/idempotency note and an Optimize export; Liam to provide traffic profile. We'll schedule the POC scoping call for Jan 21.

[00:39:00] Priya: Thanks, that was helpful. Looking forward to trying the sandbox.
[00:39:06] Liam: We'll run a smoke test and aim to get the latency numbers to you by the 22nd.
[00:39:12] Sara: And please include the Console screenshots for route fallback settings.

[00:40:00] Maya: Will do. Any final quick questions?
[00:40:05] Priya: Nope, that's it.
[00:40:10] Maya: Great — we'll follow up with the materials. Thanks everyone.
[00:40:20] [meeting ends — 40:20 recorded, ~45m scheduled]
